brief: Chair Warsh has put Fed balance-sheet reform on the agenda. Morgan Stanley's base case is roughly $1.5tr of balance-sheet reduction over about two years, starting as early as 1Q27, within a plausible $0.6tr-$2.5tr range. MS expects the Fed to keep its ample-reserves regime by cutting reserve demand (mainly tiered interest on reserve balances, plus a smaller Treasury General Account and liquidity-rule reform) roughly in step with reduced reserve supply, avoiding a shift to scarce reserves. Passive Treasury runoff (~$1tr/year) is the base case for shrinking assets, not active sales. Market impact depends on how Treasury refinances maturing SOMA holdings: bill-funded runoff, MS's expectation, returns little duration to private investors and should have limited market effect, while coupon-heavy funding would return more duration and pressure term premiums. MS assigns MBS sales a low, 15% probability, supplementing paydowns by up to $5bn/month; if pursued, that could widen lower-coupon MBS spreads 10-20bp. Warsh frames QE as having overstayed its purpose and blurred fiscal/monetary lines; MS takes the narrower, technocratic view that balance-sheet size is simply a monetary-policy instrument. Scarce reserves or MBS sales are flagged as the larger risks.
